asDecan.p: Your Sun falls between 10 and 19 degrees of Capricorn. Those ten degrees make up a decan, one of three to a sign, each with its own planet and small card, and yours is the middle one, where Capricorn has settled in and is running at full strength. In the old Chaldean order it belongs to Mars, and Mars is exalted in Capricorn, the traditional term for a planet that's an honoured guest in a sign, well treated and on its best behaviour. The hurry and temper Mars shows elsewhere get turned into steady hard work here. Saturn still owns the sign, so underneath it's cardinal earth, ambitious and patient, and Mars supplies the hands-on part. The slice before yours is the Two of Pentacles, Jupiter's, busy juggling. The one after is the Four, the Sun's, holding on to what it has. Yours is the bit in between, the man up on the bench in the picture with a chisel in his hand, still working.

You like work you can point at. The spreadsheet that finally balances, the shelf you put up that's still level three years later, the report nobody has to send back. In a meeting you're the one who asks who's actually doing each part and by when, and people find that either a relief or slightly annoying. At a family dinner you end up fixing the tap nobody mentioned. A Sunday with nothing planned usually lasts until about eleven before you've found a job, and you'd call that relaxing. You're competitive, though quietly. Nobody hears you keeping score, but you know exactly whether your half of the job came out better than the last person's. When a friend asks for help moving house you turn up with your own tape and a system for labelling the boxes.

Most people hear criticism of their work as criticism of them, and you mostly don't. Mars is exalted here, so the fight in you goes into the job itself, and when someone says the plan has a flaw your first reaction is interest. A manager marks up your draft in red and you're a bit pleased, because now it'll be better. You give feedback the same way, straight and about the thing, and people trust it because it's never really about them. That makes you very good anywhere several trades have to fit together, a building site, a hospital ward, a restaurant kitchen on a Saturday night. It also makes you a good teacher, if a slightly exacting one. Younger colleagues often remember you years later as the one who showed them how to do it properly without making them feel stupid.

You rate people by the quality of what they produce, and you're often unaware you're doing it. A colleague who's lovely but sloppy gets filed under unreliable and never quite gets out of that file. Your brother-in-law assembles the flat-pack wardrobe and you say nothing, and then, once everyone's gone to bed, you take the doors off and rehang them. That's Mars, which wants to act, meeting Saturn's sign, which wants it done to standard. The people around you notice the rehung doors. What they hear is that their help wasn't good enough, and after a few of those they stop offering. It turns inward as well. You can have a perfectly decent year and only really remember the two jobs you'd have done differently.

Bad news sends you straight to work. A redundancy, a breakup, a parent going into care, and within a day you've made a list, rung the people who need ringing and started on whatever can be fixed. That's genuinely useful, and in a crisis you're the one others lean on. By the following week the practical jobs have run out and the feeling is still sitting there, so you find new ones. You clean out the garage, take on a second project, stay back at the office. The people close to you can end up feeling shut out, because you're busy in the next room when they wanted to sit with you. What helps is something physical with no outcome, a long swim, a hard walk up a hill, turning over a garden bed that didn't need it. After that, tell one person what actually happened and how it felt.

Anyone who's gone out with you for more than a few months has had their car serviced, their gutters cleared or their CV rewritten at eleven at night, usually without asking. You also fall for competence, which people don't always spot. Someone who's very good at their job, or cooks properly, or can get an old engine going, gets your attention faster than someone who's merely charming. The best relationships for this decan usually have a shared project in them early, a house, a business, a garden, a long trip that takes planning, because working side by side is how you get close. The risk is the relationship itself becoming the project, with stages and a schedule, and a partner who starts to feel a bit managed. Physically Mars here is patient and steady, and you show desire in a plain, unfussy way that most people find reassuring.

The Devil is your Sun card, and it gives you the ambition and a clear eye for how power works in a place. This slice adds the craft underneath. You want to be very good at an actual thing, surgery or joinery or tax law or cutting hair, and you want the respect of people who can tell the difference. Trades, engineering, anything with an apprenticeship or a long training suits you, and so does any team where each person has a specialty and the job fails if one of them slacks. You tend to rise by being the one who knows how it's done. The usual mistake is staying on the tools too long. There comes a point where the business or the department needs you to plan and delegate, and you'd honestly prefer to be up the ladder doing it yourself. Take the promotion anyway, and keep one piece of hands-on work that stays yours.

Twenty-year-olds with the Sun here are usually the ones who had the part-time job all through uni, the savings account, the firm opinions about how the café should be run, and they can be hard on friends who look like they're drifting. By the mid-thirties the pattern tends to pay off in a visible way, a qualification finished, a small business with staff, a name in a narrow field. That's also when a lot of them look up and can't remember their last proper holiday. It's common to see a deliberate change around then, a new sport, a hobby with no income attached, a partner who books the leave for both of them. The fifties tend to be kind to this slice of Capricorn. The skill is deep by then, and there's often real pleasure in training someone younger and handing over part of what they made.

Pick one thing a month that someone else has done for you and let it stand exactly as they did it. The dishwasher loaded their way, the email a colleague drafted, the seedlings your partner planted too close together. Don't fix it, don't mention it, and don't quietly redo it later when they've gone out. If the itch gets strong, go and do some hard physical work on something that's only yours, sand back a chair, knead bread for ten minutes. Then thank them for it.
